prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

=== key f6ec85a2f0d2

Problem: How to run an experiment testing whether patriotic paintings can be generated without training on patriotic paintings.
Write-up text before the decision: abel photos with lots of green or blue (e.g. forest or sea or blue skies) as peaceful/calming, and so abstract art based on those colors would be labeled similarly. Red or muddy-gray colors would produce a different response. This extends beyond colors to visual textures, shapes, symmetry vs. disorder and so on. (Compare this [Rothko](https://publicdelivery.org/mark-rothko-chapel/) to this [one](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-Rothko)). > Maybe you could train an AI on patriotic paintings and then it could produce patriotic paintings, but I think only by working on theory of mind would an AI think to produce a patriotic painting without having seen one before. I agree with your general point about the relevance of theory of mind. However, I think Sensory Optimization could generate patriotic paintings without training on them. Suppose you have a dataset that's richer than ImageNet and includes human emotion and sentiment labels/captions. Some photos will cause patriotic sentiments: e.g. photos of parades or parties on national celebrations, photos of a national sports team winning, photos of iconic buildings or natural wonders. So to create patriotic paintings, you would optimize for labels relating to patriotism. If there are emotional intensity ratings for photos, and patriotic scenes cause high intensity, then maybe you could get patriotic paintings by just optimizing for intensity. (Facebook has trained models on a huge image dataset with Instagram hashtags -- some of which relate to patriotic sentiment. Someone could run a version of this experiment today.

In 2019, Metaculus posted the [results](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/2568/ragnar%25C3%25B6k-question-series-results-so-far/) of a forecasting series on catastrophic risk (>95% of humans die) by 2100. To convert this to a forecast for existential risk (100% dead), I assumed 6% risk from AI, 1% from nuclear war, and 0.4% from biological risk. Moreover, Metaculus has a separate [question](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/578/human-extinction-by-2100/) about x-risk, where the current forecast is 2% by 2100.

=== key 57ad6ff5dac5
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How to extrapolate from the >95% dead forecasts to a 100% dead forecast for different risk types.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2020-09-24, on "Forecasting Thread: Existential Risk" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/6x9rJbx9bmGsxXWEj/forecasting-thread-existential-risk-1?commentId=d5Rn2x6Z8NrsArH26 PARENT (not his words): > The overall risk was 9.2% for the community forecast (with 7.3% for AI risk). To convert this to a forecast for existential risk (100% dead), I assumed 6% risk from AI, 1% from nuclear war, and 0.4% from biological risk I think this implies you think: * AI is ~4 or 5 times (6% vs 1.3%) as likely to kill 100% of people as to kill between 95 and 100% of people * Everything other than AI is roughly equally likely (1.5% vs 1.4%) to kill 100% of people as to kill between 95% and 100% of people Does that sound right to you? And if so, what was your reasoning? I ask out of curiosity, not because I disagree. I don't have a strong view here, except perhaps that AI is the risk with the highest ratio of "chance it causes outright extinction" to "chance it causes major carnage" (and this seems to align with your views). HIS COMMENT: The Metaculus community forecast has chance of >95% dead (7.5%) close to chance of >10% dead (9.7%) for AI. Based on this and my own intuition about how AI risks "scale", I extrapolated to 6% for 100% dead. For biological and nuclear war, there's a much bigger drop off from >10% to >95% from the community. It's hard to say what to infer from this about the 100% case. There are good arguments that 100% is unlikely from both, but some of those arguments would also cut against >95%.
